hub.title: Calendar 2026–2028: Holidays, Lunar Calendar, Solar Terms and Moon Phases
hub.description: Free online calendar for 2026, 2027 and 2028: public holidays for 11 countries from official announcements, Chinese lunar dates, the 24 solar terms, full and new moons, week numbers and a solar–lunar date converter.
hub.lede: Year and month calendars with public holidays, lunar dates, solar terms and moon phases, plus a lunar date converter. Holidays are typed in from each government's own announcement.
about: Every date on these pages is worked out in your browser from tables built ahead of time: lunar months from the moment of each new moon and the 24 solar terms from the sun's position (computed with the open-source astronomy-engine library), in the standard time of each country. Nothing is looked up while you read.

Public holidays come from the official notices themselves: China's State Council, Taiwan's DGPA, the Hong Kong gazette, Japan's Cabinet Office, Korea's KASA, Vietnam's Ministry of Home Affairs, Indonesia's joint ministerial decree, the US Office of Personnel Management, GOV.UK, Spain's BOE and Mexico's Federal Labor Law. Each country page links its sources.

faq.a: Saturday, 6 February 2027 in China, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Vietnam; it starts the Year of the Goat (丁未). In Korea, which reckons the lunar calendar in UTC+9, Seollal is Sunday, 7 February 2027, because the new moon falls just before midnight Beijing time.

faq.q: How is the lunar date calculated?
faq.a: A lunar month starts on the day of a new moon in the country's standard time; the month holding the winter solstice is the 11th; in a year with 13 new moons, the first month without a major solar term is a leap month. That is why Vietnam (UTC+7), China (UTC+8) and Korea (UTC+9) occasionally start a month on different days.

Yes for the years listed on each country page: they are copied from the government announcement, including makeup working days (China's 调休) and collective leave (Indonesia's cuti bersama). Years a government has not announced yet are left out rather than guessed.

faq.q: When does Start of Spring {y} begin?
Why do the dates move by a day?
faq.a: A term is the moment the sun reaches a set longitude. The calendar year is about 365.24 days, so that moment drifts by about six hours a year and the date shifts after leap days; it also depends on the time zone.

faq.q: When are the full moons in {y}?
How many full moons are there in {y}?
Why do moon phase times differ between websites?
faq.a: The phase is one instant for the whole Earth; the date shown depends on the time zone. A full moon at 23:30 UTC is already the next day in Asia.

china: Arrangement by the General Office of the State Council for government bodies; companies generally follow it. Weekend days inside a break and the makeup working days (调休) are listed.
taiwan: The DGPA calendar for government offices. Private employers follow the Labor Standards Act, which can differ.
hong-kong: General holidays gazetted by the government. Every Sunday is also a general holiday; statutory holidays for employees are a separate, shorter list.
japan: National holidays under the Act on National Holidays, including substitute holidays (振替休日) and citizens' holidays (国民の休日).
south-korea: Public holidays of government offices (관공서의 공휴일), including substitute holidays (대체공휴일), as published in the KASA almanac.
vietnam: Statutory holidays under the Labour Code 2019. The Tết and National Day breaks shown are the Ministry of Home Affairs arrangement for public servants; companies choose their own split.
indonesia: National holidays and collective leave (cuti bersama) under the joint decree of three ministers. Islamic holiday dates can still be adjusted by decree of the Minister of Religious Affairs.
united-states: Federal holidays as listed by the Office of Personnel Management; when a holiday falls on a weekend, the observed weekday is listed too. States and private employers can differ.
united-kingdom: Bank holidays in England and Wales from GOV.UK. Scotland and Northern Ireland have different lists.
spain: Only the fiestas held in every autonomous community (BOE). Each region adds its own days, and each town adds two local ones.
mexico: Mandatory rest days under Article 74 of the Federal Labour Law. Days such as Holy Week are customary, not mandatory.
